# Erdős Problem 602: countable sets that never meet in exactly one point

*Generated by an AI agent and machine-checked (Lean file `Erdos602.lean`); not reviewed by a human expert.*

**In words.** Take any collection, of any size, of countably infinite sets. Suppose that any two of them have only
finitely many points in common, and never exactly one. Then the points can be coloured with two colours so that every
set of the collection contains both colours. This answers "yes" to a question of Komjáth published by Erdős in 1987.
Only the axiom of choice is used; no further hypothesis such as CH is needed.

Throughout, $X$ is a set, its elements are called *points*, and $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family of subsets of $X$.
*Countable* means finite or countably infinite.

**Theorem.** *Let every $A_i$ be countable with at least two points, and for all $i\ne j$ let $A_i\cap A_j$ be finite
and not have exactly one element. Then there is a colouring of the points with colours $0,1$ such that every $A_i$
contains a point of colour $0$ and a point of colour $1$.*

The statement in words is the special case in which all $A_i$ are infinite. The hypothesis on intersections is used in
two forms, always for $i\neq j$:

* **(F)** $A_i\cap A_j$ is finite;
* **(H)** if $u\in A_i\cap A_j$, then some $x\ne u$ lies in $A_i\cap A_j$.

**Idea.** Colour countably many points at a time, and call a set *split* once it contains both colours. Whenever a point
$y$ of colour $c$ lies in unsplit sets, give the opposite colour $c'$ to a set $J$ of uncoloured points that meets all
these sets and in which no point is superfluous: for every $w\in J$, one of these sets meets $J$ only in $w$. Two things
must be guaranteed: the unsplit sets still contain uncoloured points when they are needed, and the points of $J$ can be
treated in the same way later. Both follow from a simple condition: each coloured point $z$ has a *guard*, finitely many
split sets whose union contains an uncoloured point of every unsplit set through $z$. The set $J$ is taken from the sets
of the guard of $y$. Moreover the split sets carry labels: points of colour $c$ are guarded only by sets of label $c$,
and the sets that become split when $J$ is coloured get the label $c'$.

* *The points of $J$ get guards.* Here (H) enters. If $w$ is the only point of colour $c'$ in a split set $A_k$, then
  every unsplit set through $w$ meets $A_k$ in a second point. That point is uncoloured: it does not have colour $c'$,
  since $w$ is alone in $A_k$, nor colour $c$, since the set through $w$ is unsplit. So $A_k$ alone guards $w$ if its
  label is $c'$. Every $w\in J$ is such a lone point: some unsplit set through $y$ meets $J$ only in $w$. This set had no
  point of colour $c'$, since it is unsplit and contains $y$. So after the colouring of $J$ it is split, has the label
  $c'$, and has $w$ as its only point of colour $c'$.
* *The other guards survive.* A set that passes through a point of colour $c$ and is still unsplit after the colouring
  of $J$ contains no point of colour $c'$, so it has lost no uncoloured point to $J$. For points $z$ of colour $c'$ we
  must repair the loss, so it has to be finite. This is what the labels are for: $J$ lies in finitely many sets of label
  $c$, so by (F) it meets every set of label $c'$ in a finite set. Hence the guard of $z$ loses only finitely many
  points, and we add the guards of these points to it.

To start, we colour two points $v,w$ of a set without coloured points differently. If this set meets another set without
coloured points, then by (H) we can choose $v,w$ in both sets, and each of $v,w$ is guarded by one of the two sets;
otherwise $v,w$ need no guards. Dealing with one point after the other, $\omega$ times, and then using Zorn's lemma, one
reaches all sets.

## Definitions

A *partial colouring* $f$ gives some of the points $x$ a colour $f(x)\in\{0,1\}$; the other points are *uncoloured*. The
colour opposite to $c$ is $c'=1-c$. We write $f\le g$, and say that $g$ extends $f$, if every point coloured by $f$ has
the same colour under $g$. If $J$ is a set of points uncoloured by $f$, then *painting* $J$ with the colour $c$ means
passing from $f$ to the extension that gives the points of $J$ the colour $c$ and agrees with $f$ otherwise. With respect
to $f$:

* a set $A_i$ is **split** if it contains points of both colours, and **unsplit** otherwise;
* a point $y$ is **settled** if every $A_i$ containing $y$ is split;
* $f$ is **closed** if every coloured point is settled.

Let $f$ be a partial colouring, let $\ell(i)\in\{0,1\}$, $i\in I$, be arbitrary labels, and let $z$ be a point of colour
$c$. A **guard** of $z$ in $(f,\ell)$ is a finite set $G\subseteq I$ such that

* for every $k\in G$ the set $A_k$ is split and $\ell(k)=c$;
* for every unsplit $A_i$ containing $z$, the set $A_i\cap\bigcup_{k\in G}A_k$ contains an uncoloured point.

A **state** is a pair $(f,\ell)$ of a partial colouring and labels such that only countably many coloured points are
unsettled and every coloured point has a guard in $(f,\ell)$. (Guards do not involve the labels of unsplit sets.)

Four remarks follow directly from the definitions.

* **(a)** If $f\le g$, then what is split (settled) with respect to $f$ is split (settled) with respect to $g$.
* **(b)** An unsplit set containing a point of colour $c$ contains no point of colour $c'$.
* **(c)** The empty set is a guard of every settled coloured point.
* **(d)** A set of partial colourings that is totally ordered by $\le$ has a *union*: the partial colouring in which $x$
  has colour $c$ if and only if it has colour $c$ in some member. (Two members never disagree at $x$, since one of them
  extends the other.) It extends all members.

## Lemma 1 (greedy hitting set)

*Let $(F_i)_{i\in E}$ be nonempty finite sets of points. There is $J\subseteq\bigcup_i F_i$ that meets every $F_i$ and
such that every $w\in J$ has an index $i\in E$ with $F_i\cap J=\{w\}$.*

(A *hitting set* of a family is a set that meets every member, and it is *minimal* if no point can be removed from it.
So the lemma says that a family of nonempty finite sets has a minimal hitting set.)

*Proof.* Well-order the points and decide by recursion along this order which points to take: $w$ is taken if and only
if there is $i\in E$ such that $w$ is the last point of $F_i$ and no earlier point of $F_i$ was taken. Let $J$ be the set
of taken points. If $w\in J$ and $i$ is as in the rule, then $F_i\cap J=\{w\}$. Conversely let $i\in E$ and let $w$ be
the last point of $F_i$. If $w\notin J$, then by the rule some earlier point of $F_i$ was taken. So $J$ meets $F_i$.
$\square$

## Lemma 2 (lone points)

*Let $f$ be a partial colouring with labels $\ell$. Let $A_k$ be split with $\ell(k)=c$, and let $w$ be the only point of
colour $c$ in $A_k$. Then $\{k\}$ is a guard of $w$, that is, every unsplit $A_i$ containing $w$ has an uncoloured point
in $A_k$.*

*Proof.* Let $A_i$ be unsplit with $w\in A_i$. Then $i\ne k$, and (H) gives $x\ne w$ in $A_i\cap A_k$. The point $x$ does
not have colour $c$, because $w$ is the only such point of $A_k$. It does not have colour $c'$ by (b), because $A_i$ is
unsplit and contains $w$. So $x$ is uncoloured. $\square$

## Lemma 3 (settling sets)

*Let $(f,\ell)$ be a state and let $y$ be a point of colour $c$. There is a countable set $J$ of uncoloured points such
that*

1. *every unsplit $A_i$ containing $y$ meets $J$;*
2. *every $w\in J$ has an index $j$ such that $A_j$ is unsplit, $y\in A_j$ and $A_j\cap J=\{w\}$;*
3. *if $\ell(k)=c'$, then $A_k\cap J$ is finite (whether $A_k$ is split or not).*

*We call such a $J$ a settling set for $y$.*

*Proof.* Let $G$ be a guard of $y$ and let $U$ be the set of uncoloured points of $\bigcup_{k\in G}A_k$. If $i\notin G$,
then $A_i\cap U$ is finite, since by (F) it lies in the finite union of the finite sets $A_i\cap A_k$, $k\in G$.

Let $E$ be the set of all $i$ such that $A_i$ is unsplit and contains $y$. For $i\in E$ put $F_i=A_i\cap U$. This set is
nonempty because $G$ is a guard of $y$. It is finite because $i\notin G$, the members of $G$ being indices of split
sets. Take $J$ from Lemma 1. Then $J\subseteq U$, so $J$ consists of uncoloured points and is countable. (1) holds
because $J$ meets every $F_i$, $i\in E$. (2) holds because $J\subseteq U$ gives $A_j\cap J=F_j\cap J$ for $j\in E$. For
(3), the indices in $G$ have label $c$, so $k\notin G$, and $A_k\cap J\subseteq A_k\cap U$ is finite. $\square$

## Lemma 4 (settling one point)

*Let $(f,\ell)$ be a state and let $y$ be a coloured point. There is a state $(g,m)$ with $f\le g$ such that $y$ is
settled with respect to $g$.*

*Proof.* Let $c$ be the colour of $y$ and $J$ a settling set for $y$ (Lemma 3). Let $g$ arise from $f$ by painting $J$
with the colour $c'$. Put $m(i)=\ell(i)$ if $A_i$ is split with respect to $f$, and $m(i)=c'$ otherwise. So sets that
are split with respect to $f$ stay split and keep their labels.

*$y$ is settled with respect to $g$.* Let $y\in A_i$. If $A_i$ is split with respect to $f$, it stays split. Otherwise it
meets $J$ by (1), so it contains $y$ of colour $c$ and a point of colour $c'$.

*Countably many unsettled points.* Let $z$ be coloured by $g$ and unsettled with respect to $g$. Then $z$ lies in the
countable set $J$, or $z$ is coloured by $f$ and, by (a), unsettled with respect to $f$. There are only countably many
points of the second kind, since $(f,\ell)$ is a state.

*Claim.* For each $w\in J$ fix an index as in (2) and call it $q(w)$. Then $\{q(w)\}$ is a guard of $w$ in $(g,m)$.
Indeed, let $j=q(w)$. The set $A_j$ contains $y$, so it is split with respect to $g$, and $m(j)=c'$ because it was
unsplit with respect to $f$. By (b) for $f$, the set $A_j$ has no point $x$ with $f(x)=c'$, because it contains $y$.
Together with $A_j\cap J=\{w\}$ this shows that $w$ is the only point of $A_j$ with colour $c'$ under $g$. Now the claim
follows from Lemma 2.

*Guards.* Let $z$ be coloured by $g$. Then $f(z)=c$, or $z\in J$, or $f(z)=c'$.

(i) $f(z)=c$. Let $G$ be a guard of $z$ in $(f,\ell)$. It is also a guard of $z$ in $(g,m)$: its members are indices of
sets that are split with respect to $f$, and these stay split and keep the label $c$. Let $A_i$ contain $z$ and be
unsplit with respect to $g$. By (a) it is unsplit with respect to $f$, so there are $k\in G$ and $x\in A_i\cap A_k$
uncoloured by $f$. By (b) for $g$, the set $A_i$ has no point of colour $c'$, so $x\notin J$. Hence $x$ is uncoloured by
$g$.

(ii) $z\in J$. By the claim, $\{q(z)\}$ is a guard of $z$ in $(g,m)$.

(iii) $f(z)=c'$. Let $H$ be a guard of $z$ in $(f,\ell)$, and let $T=J\cap\bigcup_{k\in H}A_k$. The set $H$ is finite,
and its members have label $c'$, so each $A_k\cap J$ with $k\in H$ is finite by (3). Hence $T$ is finite. We show that
the finite set $H\cup\{q(w):w\in T\}$ is a guard of $z$ in $(g,m)$. Its members are indices of sets that are split with
respect to $g$ and have label $c'$ under $m$: for $k\in H$ as in (i), for $q(w)$ by the claim. Let $A_i$ contain $z$ and
be unsplit with respect to $g$, hence also with respect to $f$. Then there are $k\in H$ and $x\in A_i\cap A_k$ uncoloured
by $f$. If $x\notin J$, then $x$ is uncoloured by $g$. If $x\in J$, then $x\in T$, and by the claim $\{q(x)\}$ is a guard
of $x$ in $(g,m)$. Since $A_i$ contains $x$ and is unsplit with respect to $g$, it has a point in $A_{q(x)}$ that is
uncoloured by $g$. $\square$

## Lemma 5 (closing off)

*For every state $(f,\ell)$ there is a closed partial colouring $g\ge f$.*

*Proof.* Let $\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$, and let $(p,r)\mapsto\langle p,r\rangle$ be a bijection from
$\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$ to $\mathbb N$ with $p\le\langle p,r\rangle$, for example
$\langle p,r\rangle=2^p(2r+1)-1$. For every state enumerate its unsettled coloured points by natural numbers $0,1,\dots$;
the list may be infinite, finite or empty. Define states $s_0=(f,\ell),s_1,s_2,\dots$ with colourings
$f_0\le f_1\le\dots$ as follows. Let $n=\langle p,r\rangle$; then $p\le n$, so $s_p$ is already defined. If the list of
$s_p$ has an entry $y$ with number $r$, then $y$ is coloured by $f_p$, hence by $f_n$, and we let $s_{n+1}$ be a state
given by Lemma 4 for $s_n$ and $y$. Otherwise let $s_{n+1}=s_n$.

Let $g$ be the union of the $f_n$ (remark (d)). Let $y$ be coloured by $g$, hence by some $f_p$. If $y$ is settled with
respect to $f_p$, then also with respect to $g$, by (a). If not, then $y$ has a number $r$ on the list of $s_p$. For
$n=\langle p,r\rangle$ it is settled with respect to $f_{n+1}$, hence with respect to $g$. $\square$

## Lemma 6 (starting)

*Let $f$ be a closed partial colouring and let $A_a$ be unsplit with respect to $f$. There is a state $(g,m)$ with
$f\le g$ such that $A_a$ is split with respect to $g$.*

*Proof.* A set that is unsplit with respect to $f$ has no point coloured by $f$, because $f$ is closed. For any two
points $v\ne w$ of $A_a$ let $g$ arise from $f$ by painting $v$ with $0$ and $w$ with $1$. Every set containing $v$ and
$w$, in particular $A_a$, is split with respect to $g$. The points coloured by $f$ are settled with respect to $f$, hence
by (a) with respect to $g$, so they have the empty guard by (c), and at most $v$ and $w$ are coloured by $g$ and
unsettled. It remains to choose $v,w$ and labels $m$ such that $v$ and $w$ have guards in $(g,m)$.

*First case: some $A_b$ with $b\ne a$ is unsplit with respect to $f$ and meets $A_a$.* By (H) we can choose $v\ne w$ in
$A_a\cap A_b$. Put $m(a)=0$ and $m(i)=1$ for $i\ne a$. With respect to $g$ the sets $A_a$ and $A_b$ are split. As neither
has a point coloured by $f$, the point $v$ is the only one of colour $0$ in $A_a$, and $w$ is the only one of colour $1$
in $A_b$. By Lemma 2, $\{a\}$ is a guard of $v$ and $\{b\}$ is a guard of $w$.

*Second case: there is no such $b$.* Choose any $v\ne w$ in $A_a$ and any labels. An $A_i$ with $i\ne a$ that contains
$v$ or $w$ meets $A_a$, so it is split with respect to $f$, hence with respect to $g$. Therefore $v$ and $w$ are settled
with respect to $g$ and have the empty guard. $\square$

## Proof of the Theorem

Order the closed partial colourings by $\le$. The union of a chain of closed partial colourings is closed: a point
coloured by the union is coloured, hence settled, in some member, hence settled in the union. (The union of the empty
chain colours no point.) By Zorn's lemma there is a maximal closed partial colouring $f$. Suppose that some $A_a$ is
unsplit with respect to $f$. Lemma 6 gives a state $(g,m)$ with $f\le g$ in which $A_a$ is split, and Lemma 5 gives a
closed $h$ with $f\le g\le h$. The set $A_a$ is split with respect to $h$, so $h\neq f$, against the maximality of $f$.
Hence every $A_i$ is split with respect to $f$. Give the uncoloured points colour $0$. $\square$

## What is new and what is borrowed

The question is Komjáth's [1]. Known before: the finite case [2]; countable families, and families with a minimal
hitting set or with a well-ordering of the points in which every set has a last point [3, 4, 5]; uniformly bounded
intersections [6, 7, 8]. Lemma 1 is not new: see [3, 4, 9], and [10] for the dual statement, with the roles of points
and sets exchanged. In Lean, with Zorn's lemma, it is in pull request 1290 of grandchallenge/MATHSOLVE by GitHub user
fyremael (2026, MIT licence), which was read before this work started. The use of (H) for a hitting set each point of
which is alone in some set (Lemma 2 and the claim in Lemma 4) is Lovász's idea [2]; see also [3, 5]. Carrying out
countably many tasks one after the other, as in Lemma 5, is the method of Bernstein's lemma (countably many infinite
sets have such a colouring). What appears to be new is the combination, that is, the guards and labels that let these
steps be repeated without a minimal hitting set for the whole family. New as far as known: two limited searches (24–25
November 2026) found no proof of the full statement and no published theorem implying it. They are not a certificate of
novelty; in particular the full text of [11] and the discussion page of the problem were not seen. Of [11] only the
abstract was read, and nothing in the abstract claims the present theorem. More references and caveats are in the header
of the Lean file.

1. P. Erdős, *Some problems on finite and infinite graphs*, Contemp. Math. 65 (1987) 223–228, item 12, p. 227.
2. L. Lovász, *Combinatorial Problems and Exercises*, Problem 13.33.
3. R. Ahlswede, L. H. Khachatrian, *Splitting properties in partially ordered sets and set systems* (preprint 1994), in:
   Numbers, Information and Complexity, Kluwer 2000, 29–44.
4. Péter L. Erdős, *Splitting property in infinite posets*, Discrete Math. 163 (1997) 251–256.
5. Péter L. Erdős, L. Soukup, *How to split antichains in infinite posets*, Combinatorica 27 (2007) 147–161.
6. E. W. Miller, C. R. Soc. Sci. Lett. Varsovie 30 (1937) 31–38 (cited second-hand, like [7] and [8]).
7. P. Erdős, A. Hajnal, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 12 (1961) 87–123.
8. P. Komjáth, Acta Math. Hungar. 43 (1984) 199–207.
9. P. Komjáth, Discrete Math. 342 (2019) 1849–1856 (only a review was read).
10. J. Klimó, Discrete Appl. Math. 45 (1993) 161–168 (as quoted in [3]).
11. P. Komjáth, *Set systems with finite chromatic number*, European J. Combin. 10 (1989) 543–549.
